articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbreak in 2026 marks the third human BDBV event, following Uganda (2007–08; 131 cases, 42 deaths) and DR Congo (2012; 38 cases, 13 deaths). It reached regional proportions and triggered a health emergency of international concern; unlike Ebola, BDBV has no licensed vaccines or validated therapies. Two EBOV-targeted monoclonal antibodies (Inmazeb, Ebanga) show improved survival for Ebola but their activity against BDBV is unknown. Historical case fatality ranges 30–50%, though current CFR may reflect detection bias toward severe cases. Bayesian phylogeny identifies two clades (UGA, COD); new sequences cluster near COD, with no evidence of independent zoonotic introductions. Early BDBV symptoms resemble other febrile illnesses; the index nurse in Bunia (April 24, 2026) went over three weeks undiagnosed, enabling spread to Kampala and Kinshasa; sequencing confirmed BDBV by May 15, 2026. The article proposes a cognition gap—need for AI-powered infrastructure to synthesize diverse data and inform decisions.

articleHeadline: Why are children most vulnerable to Chandipura virus? Doctor explain the hidden risk
articleSummary: Chandipura virus in India continues to cause fatal and severe infections predominantly in children under five, with several child deaths reported in rural and forested regions. The virus rapidly targets the brain, causing acute encephalitis, seizures, unconsciousness, breathing difficulties, paralysis, or coma. Young children are especially vulnerable due to an immature blood–brain barrier and rapid brain development, and increased exposure to sandflies because of ground-level play in areas where sandflies are common. Early symptoms are often missed because toddlers cannot articulate them; warning signs include sudden excessive sleepiness, feeding refusal, loss of head control, weak limbs, seizures, vomiting, or reduced responsiveness—requiring urgent medical care. Survivors may suffer long-term neurodevelopmental issues; early rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, developmental assessment) started during hospitalization can improve outcomes. There is no specific antiviral; prevention centers on reducing sandfly exposure.

Health consequences included anxiety and depression; economically, unemployment, poverty, GDP contraction, disrupted supply chains, and prolonged school closures with a shift to virtual education. articleHeadline: Climate change set to redraw Africa's malaria map, study finds
articleSummary: By 2050, rising temperatures are projected to expand the range of malaria-carrying mosquitoes into cooler parts of southern and eastern Africa, per a Nature study. Coastal southern Africa could see malaria cases rise up to 20%, while the East African highlands (including parts of Kenya and Ethiopia) and areas in Angola, Zambia and eastern South Africa could see about a 5% increase. In hotter regions, transmission may fall roughly 5% in Nigeria, Burkina Faso and Mali, while parts of the Sahel could become too hot for mosquitoes, potentially eliminating malaria there. In South Africa, three north-eastern provinces are most at risk, underscoring the need for strengthened local malaria control. Africa recorded about 579,000 malaria deaths in 2024, three-quarters of them children under five. Limiting warming to 2 C could prevent additional malaria cases, especially in southern Africa and East African highlands, but requires stronger surveillance and control.
notes: 本記事はNature誌掲載の将来予測研究（2050年時点でのマラリア流行地域変化）を紹介する内容であり、特定国での現在進行中のアウトブレイクを報じるものではない。複数国（南アフリカ、アンゴラ、ザンビア、エチオピア、ケニア、ナイジェリア、ブルキナファソ、マリ）が予測モデルの対象として並列的に言及されているが、いずれも記事の主題として単独で扱われていないため、地域検証ルールに基づきverified_locationsは空とした。

articleSummary: New Delhi, 2026-08-04: Chandipura virus has caused 22 child deaths in Gujarat during the current monsoon season, with 35 confirmed infections among 184 suspected cases; 11 suspected samples remain pending. Chandipura virus is an uncommon member of the Rhabdoviridae family (Vesiculovirus genus), first detected in 1965 near Nagpur, Maharashtra. articleSummary: Climate change could eliminate malaria from West and Central Africa as rising temperatures exceed Anopheles mosquito tolerances, per Nature via Science in Poland. Malaria, caused by Plasmodium, killed about 610,000 people in 2024 across 80 countries. Laboratory data show optimal mosquito/parasite survival at 16–34°C, with peak transmission near 26°C. Tamma Carleton and colleagues aggregated over 50,000 Sub-Saharan African malaria studies (1900–2016) into 9,875 monthly provincial averages and modeled climate scenarios. They found that recent warming contributed roughly 1 extra malaria case per 1,000 people (2010–2014), concentrated in West and Central Africa. Under high-emission futures, by 2100 West Africa could see about 45 fewer cases per 1,000 children; the Democratic Republic of the Congo about 16 fewer per 1,000. articleHeadline: WHO warns DR Congo's Ebola outbreak outpaces response
articleSummary: The World Health Organization warned that the Democratic Republic of the Congo's Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has expanded beyond current response capabilities, becoming the country's largest crisis. As of Aug. 1, 3,748 confirmed cases and 1,657 deaths have occurred across 49 health zones in five provinces, with 708 recoveries. About 17,000 contacts remain under active monitoring, and health workers are following up on more than 80% of cases daily. There are no proven safe or effective treatments or vaccines specifically for Bundibugyo at present, though supportive care can save lives. Experimental treatments and a potential post-exposure preventive medicine are in trials in Congo; two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines have entered Phase 1 trials in the UK and Canada. Safe burial teams and community health workers require additional resources to prevent further transmission.

articleHeadline: Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital patient likely contracted Legionnaires' Disease from hospital water dispenser
articleSummary: Legionnaires' disease likely contracted by a patient at Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital from a contaminated hospital water dispenser. On 4 August 2026, the Centre for Health Protection (CHP) said the source was a cooled boiled-water device (BC-Tap Classic BA-Heat Exchange) supplied by Aqua Vital Water Filtration Systems Ltd. Water samples from the device outlet tested positive for Legionella pneumophila non-serogroup 1 at 3–16.6 CFU/mL, above the 0.1 CFU/mL action level; sequence-based typing matched the strain in the patient’s respiratory specimen. The hospital stopped using the device, provided bottled water, and disinfected the ward water system under CHP instruction. 137 patients on the same floor are under medical surveillance; none has developed Legionnaires' disease so far. A wider survey found four positive water samples and one positive environmental sample in identical devices (0.3–12.9 CFU/mL). A CHP-EMSD investigation linked the risk to a built-in cooling conduit with infrequent disinfection that can harbor warm stagnant water; infection occurs via inhalation of contaminated droplets or mist from artificial water systems. Advisory actions and ongoing investigations are in place.

articleSummary: Haemaphysalis longicornis, the Asian longhorned tick, is a major vector for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTS), Rickettsia, and Theileria, and its bite can trigger meat allergy in humans. Originating in East Asia (Japan, Korea, China), it has spread to Oceania and was first detected in the United States in 2017. In a genetic study by Ryo Nakao and colleagues, complete mitochondrial genomes and SNPs were analyzed from Japan, Fiji, New Caledonia, and Australia, plus five laboratory lines (two sexually reproducing, three parthenogenetic). The mitochondrial phylogeny shows two main clades aligned with reproductive mode, supporting a globally distributed parthenogenetic lineage, though three males were observed within this clade. SNP analyses reveal gene flow between clades, suggesting parthenogenesis evolved multiple times. Published in PNAS Nexus, the study provides genetic context to tracking and preventing the spread of this invasive tick.

articleSummary: Malaria transmission in Africa is reshaped by climate change, with rising risk in parts of southern and eastern Africa while declines occur in some current hotspots. articleSummary: On 2026-08-04, the WHO warns that the largest Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo's history is spiraling beyond control and requires greater international support. Since the outbreak was declared on 15 May, there have been 3,802 confirmed Ebola virus disease cases and 1,707 deaths, with 727 recoveries reported and roughly 17,000 people under surveillance due to exposure to the virus. The northeastern Ituri province bears the brunt, accounting for about 90% of cases. The outbreak is driven by the Bundibugyo strain, for which no proven safe and effective vaccine or therapy exists at present. Ongoing evaluations of new therapies and vaccines are underway, with initial results described as encouraging by the WHO.

articleHeadline: Moderna's Ebola vaccine trial targets a strain with no cure
articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is driving the second-deadliest outbreak on record, with roughly 3,750 confirmed cases and more than 1,650 deaths as of Aug. 1. Moderna launched a Phase 1 trial of mRNA-1469, an experimental vaccine targeting Bundibugyo, at three Canadian sites (Halifax and Truro in Nova Scotia, and Toronto) enrolling about 80 healthy adults; first participants received injections on Aug. 4, 2026. Canada is the second country after the UK to test a Bundibugyo vaccine candidate. The trial assesses safety, tolerability and immune response, not efficacy. CEPI-funded, up to $50 million, with parallel manufacturing to accelerate later trials; Moderna pledges at least 500,000 doses to low- and middle-income countries if licensed. Cross-protection from Zaire EBOV vaccines may be possible; Uganda reported 20 cases and 2 deaths linked to the Congo outbreak, with ongoing regional risk.
notes: 記事本文はカナダでのモデルナ製ブンディブギョ株エボラワクチンの第1相治験開始が主題だが、背景として現在進行中のDRCにおける大規模エボラ流行（史上2番目の致死性）が主要な公衆衛生イベントである。ウガンダへの拡大も報告されているが、ウガンダは対象国リストに含まれないため verified_locations には含めない。カナダも同様に対象国リスト外。

articleSummary: Anopheles stephensi, an invasive malaria-carrying mosquito, is expanding rapidly across Africa and showing resistance to all insecticides used in vector control. Genomic analysis of samples from ten countries confirms resistance to common chemicals used in spraying and other programs. First detected in Djibouti over a decade ago, the species has advanced west to Ghana and south through Kenya, inhabiting both urban and rural areas and remaining active in dry seasons. Researchers warn containment may be unlikely; eradicating the mosquito could be unfeasible. Unlike other African malaria vectors, A. stephensi thrives in cities such as Lagos and Kinshasa, potentially elevating urban malaria risk. Malaria remains a leading killer in Africa, with ongoing studies to curb transmission. An imported case: a 37-year-old Moscow region resident developed malaria after a Zanzibar, Tanzania trip; fever, joint pain, weakness, fever spikes; prophylaxis not taken; malaria diagnosed. The couple were frequently bitten by mosquitoes during the trip.

articleHeadline: Malaria Causes Permanent Damage to Phagocytes in the Spleen Macrophages formed in the bone marrow can only assume the function of embryonal phagocytes, or "scavenger cells," to a certain degree according to a study by the University of Bonn and the Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity at the University of Melbourne. articleSummary: Malaria infection permanently damages splenic CD163 macrophages, the resident phagocytes that clear aged red blood cells and recycle iron. Replacing cells from the bone marrow does not restore the original specialization, leaving the signaling to the marginal zone disrupted. CD163 macrophages coordinate immune messages to the spleen’s marginal zone; their depletion weakens this network and can lead to more severe infection, higher parasitemia, and longer anemia, with worse outcomes on repeat infections. Because CD163 macrophages exist in humans, the findings imply malaria could permanently alter immunological memory and iron metabolism, potentially affecting vaccine effectiveness in endemic regions.
